title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular Assessment
html:
A cardiovascular and peripheral vascular assessment asks whether the heart is moving blood effectively and whether tissues are receiving adequate perfusion. The RN integrates the client’s symptoms with blood pressure and pulse trends, level of consciousness, skin findings, heart sounds, jugular veins, peripheral pulses, capillary refill, edema, movement, and sensation. A single finding rarely explains the cause; patterns, change from baseline, and acuity determine the response.

Learning goals

  • Collect a focused cardiovascular and peripheral vascular history.
  • Inspect the precordium, neck veins, skin, and extremities systematically.
  • Auscultate heart sounds at standard landmarks and assess apical rate and rhythm.
  • Compare peripheral pulses and tissue-perfusion findings safely.
  • Describe edema and recognize urgent arterial, venous, and cardiac warning patterns.
  • Document objective findings, actions, communication, and reassessment.

Begin with stability and time-sensitive symptoms

Observe appearance, breathing, speech, position, skin color and moisture, movement, and responsiveness before focusing on the chest. Review blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm, respiratory rate, oxygenation, pain, recent procedures, medications, intake and output, weight trend, activity tolerance, and reliable baseline. Signs of poor perfusion can appear in the brain, skin, kidneys, lungs, and extremities as well as in pulse measurements.

New chest pressure or discomfort with dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, syncope, hypotension, or altered mental status requires immediate assessment and the appropriate emergency pathway. Other urgent patterns include a suddenly cool, pale, painful, numb, or pulseless extremity; uncontrolled bleeding; severe dyspnea with new edema or crackles; or unilateral leg swelling followed by sudden chest symptoms. Stabilization and escalation take priority over completing the routine sequence.

Do not wait for a classic description
Potentially serious cardiovascular problems may be reported as pressure, tightness, burning, indigestion, unusual fatigue, breathlessness, weakness, dizziness, or upper-body discomfort. Assess the entire symptom cluster and change from baseline rather than requiring the client to use the word “pain.”

Ask a focused cardiovascular history

Use a symptom structure such as PQRSTU to explore chest discomfort: onset, provoking or relieving factors, quality, region and radiation, severity, timing, associated symptoms, prior episodes, treatments, and the client’s understanding. Ask about palpitations, skipped or racing beats, dizziness, fainting, dyspnea at rest or with exertion, shortness of breath when lying flat, waking breathless, cough, fatigue, reduced activity tolerance, swelling, rapid weight change, and decreased urine output.

For peripheral circulation, ask about limb pain, heaviness, cramping with activity, pain at rest, temperature or color change, numbness, tingling, wounds, delayed healing, and whether symptoms are unilateral. Review cardiovascular and vascular history, diabetes and other relevant conditions, recent immobility or procedures, pregnancy or postpartum status when relevant, tobacco and nicotine exposure, family history, and prescribed medications such as antihypertensives, diuretics, antiarrhythmics, antiplatelets, or anticoagulants. Verify adherence and adverse effects without blame.

Inspect the client and circulation

Assess level of consciousness and respiratory effort. Inspect the face, lips, oral mucosa, hands, and feet for pallor or cyanosis using appropriate lighting and multiple sites across skin tones. Note diaphoresis. Look at the precordium for scars, implanted-device contours, deformity, or visible pulsations without assuming their meaning.

With the client positioned about 30 to 45 degrees when tolerated, inspect the neck for jugular venous distention and observe symmetry and tracheal alignment. Position, body habitus, lighting, and technique influence visibility. A neck-vein finding is a cue to integrate with breathing, lung sounds, edema, weight, urine output, and hemodynamic status—not a stand-alone diagnosis.

Inspect both upper and lower extremities for color, warmth, movement, sensation, hair distribution, swelling, superficial veins, wounds, and device or dressing effects. Compare corresponding sides. Unilateral and bilateral changes suggest different patterns, but neither should be diagnosed from inspection alone.

Auscultate rate, rhythm, and heart sounds

Use a quiet environment and place the stethoscope directly on the skin. A common landmark sequence covers the aortic, pulmonic, Erb’s point, tricuspid, and mitral or apical areas. These names identify listening locations; they are not the exact anatomic positions of the valves. Use the diaphragm for higher-pitched sounds and the bell lightly for lower-pitched sounds as taught and within policy.

At each site, identify rate, rhythm, S1 and S2, and any extra sound, murmur, click, or rub. Describe the sound and location; do not independently assign the underlying structural diagnosis. Count the apical pulse for a full minute when the rhythm is irregular, the client is an infant or young child as appropriate, or accurate medication-related assessment is required. If an apical-radial comparison is indicated, follow the validated procedure and organizational policy.

An irregular rhythm, newly changed rate, extra sound, or murmur should be paired with symptoms, blood pressure, perfusion, medications, electrolyte or other relevant results, and prior findings. A new irregular rhythm with hypotension, chest discomfort, dyspnea, syncope, or altered mental status is more urgent than an isolated stable finding.

Assess pulses and peripheral perfusion

Palpate accessible pulses with finger pads rather than the thumb. Compare corresponding radial, brachial, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses for presence, rate, rhythm, and amplitude using the organization’s grading scale. Assess carotid pulses one side at a time; simultaneous carotid palpation can reduce cerebral blood flow. Avoid excessive pressure and follow precautions for known vascular disease.

If a peripheral pulse is difficult to feel, reposition the limb, confirm the landmark, compare the other side, and use a Doppler device when trained and permitted. Do not repeatedly compress tissue or document a pulse as absent until the appropriate focused assessment is completed. A newly absent pulse with pain, pallor, coolness, weakness, numbness, or delayed capillary refill is an urgent perfusion threat.

Assess temperature, color, movement, sensation, and capillary refill with the limb appropriately positioned. Capillary refill is affected by temperature, lighting, technique, age, and peripheral perfusion; interpret it with pulse quality and the rest of the examination. A warm room or a single reassuring refill time does not cancel severe pain or a missing pulse.

Describe edema instead of merely naming it

Inspect and palpate for edema, comparing sides and dependent areas. Record location, laterality, extent, skin condition, and whether it is pitting or nonpitting. If pitting is present, use the organization’s approved grading method consistently rather than assuming that all numeric scales are identical. Measure limb circumference at a reproducible landmark only when indicated, and record the method and side.

Interpret edema with timing, weight trend, dyspnea, lung sounds, jugular veins, urine output, mobility, medications, wounds, and recent procedures. New bilateral edema with breathlessness may reflect a different risk pattern from unilateral warmth, tenderness, redness, or swelling. Suspected venous thrombosis requires prompt evaluation; do not massage the limb or use an unvalidated maneuver to rule it in or out.

Connect the heart, lungs, brain, kidneys, and limbs

Cardiovascular assessment is multisystem. Reduced cardiac output or impaired circulation may present as confusion, restlessness, cool or mottled skin, weak pulses, delayed refill, low urine output, fatigue, dyspnea, crackles, or reduced activity tolerance. Conversely, pain, fever, dehydration, anxiety, medications, and other conditions can alter heart rate and perfusion findings. Analyze clusters rather than anchoring on the first cue.

When a concerning change appears, validate technique only if doing so does not delay care. Obtain relevant vital signs, compare with baseline, complete a focused assessment, protect the client from falls or exertion, initiate actions permitted by orders or protocol, communicate urgency and supporting data, and evaluate the response.

Respect delegation boundaries

Assistive personnel may obtain selected vital signs, weights, intake and output, or report observed swelling for a stable client when policy and competency allow. The RN decides what assessment is needed, validates unexpected data, auscultates and interprets heart and vascular findings, evaluates symptoms, prioritizes risk, communicates changes, and reassesses outcomes. Concerning delegated data must return to the RN for timely clinical judgment.

Document a reproducible vascular picture

Record symptoms and onset; vital signs and position; apical rate and rhythm; S1 and S2 and the location and character of unexpected sounds; neck-vein findings with position; pulse site, side, and grade; skin color and temperature; capillary refill; movement and sensation; edema location, laterality, pitting method or measurement; wounds; focused actions; communication; and response. Avoid vague entries such as “circulation good” or “edema present.”

For example: “1035: New right-foot pain 8/10 with pallor and coolness compared with left; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses not palpable and no Doppler signal obtained per unit procedure. Capillary refill delayed; movement present, sensation decreased. Client maintained at rest; provider and rapid-response team notified at 1038. RN remained with client; repeat neurovascular findings unchanged at 1043.” This documents the threat and response without declaring an unconfirmed diagnosis.

Clinical example

A client reports “indigestion” and unusual fatigue. The RN notices diaphoresis and a new drop in blood pressure. Rather than offering food and continuing the routine assessment, the RN clarifies onset and associated symptoms, assesses airway, breathing, circulation, mental status and perfusion, obtains immediate assistance, initiates the approved chest-symptom pathway, and reassesses continuously. The label the client chose did not lower the urgency of the cue cluster.
